analysis.one_liner: Makes giant data centers pay their own power costs and offers tax credits for new generation and water recycling.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2026 with zero cosponsors, the bill was referred to two House committees and no further action appears in the record.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill writes a federal rule that electric customers using 100 megawatts or more — essentially large data centers — must pay the full cost of any power plant, transmission, or distribution upgrades needed to serve them, and must post money up front before those upgrades are built. To soften the blow and spread the benefit, it offers a 30% tax credit when data centers build extra generating capacity that is contracted out to utilities serving homes, farms, and small businesses, and another 30% credit for water recycling systems at data centers, factories, and municipal water systems. States would have to hold proceedings on the new rule but could ultimately decline to adopt it.
analysis.who_benefits: Residential, agricultural, and small-business electric customers, who would stop subsidizing grid upgrades triggered by data centers; water users near data centers, since recycled water would replace rivers, streams, and groundwater; electric utilities, which gain required financial assurances from large loads; and data center and power-generation developers, which gain a 30% credit for surplus generation sold to other customers and for water reuse projects.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households and small businesses facing data-center-driven power costs

how_it_helps.text: Utilities would have to charge any customer drawing 100 megawatts or more the full incremental cost of the generation, transmission, and distribution upgrades needed to serve it — including if the customer later cancels its contract — and would have to collect financial assurances before building those upgrades, so those costs stop flowing to ordinary ratepayers.

Utilities would have to consider rate structures that push large-load customers to build new generation dedicated to their own demand, with any surplus capacity offered through long-term contracts to utilities serving residential, agricultural, and small-business customers.

A new 30% investment tax credit would apply to new generation capacity that exceeds a data center's own projected demand (up to 50% of it), provided the surplus is contracted for at least 10 years to utilities serving existing customers — with the credit clawed back if the data center's demand grows or the contract is cut short.

A second 30% credit would fund water recycling: onsite systems at data centers and industrial facilities, switching industrial users from groundwater and freshwater to municipal recycled water, and building or expanding municipal water recycling systems, which the bill's findings say protects aquifers.

State regulators would have to open proceedings on the large-load cost rule within one year and decide within two, though states that already have a comparable standard, a pending proceeding, or a legislative vote would be exempt.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through a 30% investment credit with no dollar cap in the bill text for surplus-generation and water-reuse projects over a 10-year window; state regulators, which must run new proceedings; and data center developers, which would bear full upfront infrastructure costs and post financial assurances, partially offset by the credits.

drawbacks.text: The ratepayer protection is not guaranteed: under the federal procedure the bill uses, state regulators must consider the standard and make a determination, but they can decline to adopt it after hearings, so households end up protected only where states choose to act.
The two 30% tax credits carry no overall dollar limit or pay-for in the bill, so the full cost to the Treasury is open-ended and would fall on taxpayers.

The water-reuse credit directly subsidizes private facilities' own water systems — including data centers' onsite recycling for their own operations — so some of the money would cover infrastructure companies would arguably need anyway.

The generation credit is only usable on projects of 100 megawatts or more tied to a large-load campus, a scale only the largest developers can finance, so the subsidy would flow disproportionately to the biggest tech and power companies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — making 100-megawatt-plus customers pay the full incremental cost of their own grid upgrades — addresses a real and growing pocketbook problem, and tying the generation credit to capacity actually contracted out to communities is more targeted than a blanket subsidy. But the protections depend on state regulators choosing to adopt them, and the credits are uncapped, last 10 years, and partly subsidize private infrastructure. On balance a reasonably designed bill whose benefits to households are real but conditional, and whose costs to taxpayers are unquantified.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late June 2026, sent to two House committees, and has sat there ever since — no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Baumgartner introduced the bill on June 24, 2026.

The Speaker referred it the same day to both the Ways and Means Committee, which handles tax credits, and the Energy and Commerce Committee, which handles utility law — a dual referral that requires two committees to act.
No member of either party signed on as a cosponsor, and no markup, hearing, or floor action appears in the record after the referral.
With the 119th Congress scheduled to end on January 3, 2027, the bill has roughly six months of session life left and no visible movement.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, the existing arrangement continues: states decide case by case whether data centers cover the grid costs they trigger, and large data center developers avoid a uniform federal requirement to pay full incremental infrastructure costs and post financial assurances. Taxpayers are also spared the uncapped credits so far.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data center developers and the status quo

for.name: Rep. Michael Baumgartner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 24, 2026 and made the case in its findings that large data-center loads should bear their full incremental infrastructure costs rather than blanket restrictions being imposed.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 24, 2026; no markup, hearing, or vote on the bill appears in the record since.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and not a single cosponsor from either party signed on, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Data centers and hyperscale cloud companies
industries.note: They would have to pay the full incremental cost of grid upgrades and post financial assurances, but they gain 30% credits for surplus generation and water recycling, plus a federal framework whose stated policy rejects blanket moratoria on data center development.
The bill requires large loads to pre-fund upgrades, cutting utilities' stranded-cost risk, and lets utilities earn credits on new generation whose excess capacity is sold to their other customers.

A new 30% investment credit rewards building generation tied to large-load campuses as long as the surplus capacity is contracted for 10 or more years to utilities serving homes, farms, and small businesses.

industries.industry: Municipal water and water recycling providers
industries.note: A 30% credit covers building or expanding municipal water recycling systems and switching industrial customers from freshwater to recycled water.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee action more than a month after referral, and two committees that would each need to act, the bill is very likely to die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress without ever reaching the floor — the fate of most bills referred to multiple committees with no cosponsors.
